go_terms.name: transcription coregulator activity
go_terms.definition: A transcription regulator activity that modulates the transcription of specific gene sets via binding to a DNA-binding transcription factor at a specific genomic locus, either on its own or as part of a complex. Coregulators often act by altering chromatin structure and modifications. For example, one class of transcription coregulators modifies chromatin structure through covalent modification of histones. A second class remodels the conformation of chromatin in an ATP-dependent fashion. A third class modulates interactions of DNA-bound DNA-binding transcription factors with other transcription coregulators.

go_terms.name: transcription coactivator activity
go_terms.definition: A transcription coregulator activity that activates or increases the transcription of specific gene sets via binding to a DNA-binding transcription factor at a specific genomic locus, either on its own or as part of a complex. Coactivators often act by altering chromatin structure and modifications. For example, one class of transcription coactivators modifies chromatin structure through covalent modification of histones. A second class remodels the conformation of chromatin in an ATP-dependent fashion. A third class modulates interactions of DNA-bound DNA-binding transcription factors with other transcription coregulators. A fourth class of coactivator activity is the bridging of a DNA-binding transcription factor to the general (basal) transcription machinery. The Mediator complex, which bridges sequence-specific DNA binding transcription factors and RNA polymerase, is also a transcription coactivator.

go_terms.name: mediator complex
go_terms.definition: A protein complex that interacts with the carboxy-terminal domain of the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II and plays an active role in transducing the signal from a transcription factor to the transcriptional machinery. The mediator complex is required for activation of transcription of most protein-coding genes, but can also act as a transcriptional corepressor. The Saccharomyces complex contains several identifiable subcomplexes: a head domain comprising Srb2, -4, and -5, Med6, -8, and -11, and Rox3 proteins; a middle domain comprising Med1, -4, and -7, Nut1 and -2, Cse2, Rgr1, Soh1, and Srb7 proteins; a tail consisting of Gal11p, Med2p, Pgd1p, and Sin4p; and a regulatory subcomplex comprising Ssn2, -3, and -8, and Srb8 proteins. Metazoan mediator complexes have similar modular structures and include homologs of yeast Srb and Med proteins.

go_terms.name: spliceosomal complex
go_terms.definition: Any of a series of ribonucleoprotein complexes that contain snRNA(s) and small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs), and are formed sequentially during the spliceosomal splicing of one or more substrate RNAs, and which also contain the RNA substrate(s) from the initial target RNAs of splicing, the splicing intermediate RNA(s), to the final RNA products. During cis-splicing, the initial target RNA is a single, contiguous RNA transcript, whether mRNA, snoRNA, etc., and the released products are a spliced RNA and an excised intron, generally as a lariat structure. During trans-splicing, there are two initial substrate RNAs, the spliced leader RNA and a pre-mRNA.

These are typically named after the snRNA(s) they contain, e.g. U1 snRNP, U4/U6 snRNP, or 7SK snRNP. Many, of these complexes become part of the spliceosome involved in splicing of nuclear mRNAs. Others are involved in regulation of transcription elongation or 3'-end processing of replication-dependent histone pre-mRNAs.

go_terms.name: U2-type prespliceosome
go_terms.definition: A spliceosomal complex that is formed by association of the 5' splice site with the U1 snRNP, while the branch point sequence is recognized by the U2 snRNP. The prespliceosome includes many proteins in addition to those found in the U1 and U2 snRNPs. Commitment to a given pair of 5' and 3' splice sites occurs at the time of prespliceosome formation.

go_terms.name: catalytic step 2 spliceosome
go_terms.definition: A spliceosomal complex that contains three snRNPs, including U5, bound to a splicing intermediate in which the first catalytic cleavage of the 5' splice site has occurred. The precise subunit composition differs significantly from that of the catalytic step 1, or activated, spliceosome, and includes many proteins in addition to those found in the associated snRNPs.

go_terms.name: microtubule
go_terms.definition: Any of the long, generally straight, hollow tubes of internal diameter 12-15 nm and external diameter 24 nm found in a wide variety of eukaryotic cells; each consists (usually) of 13 protofilaments of polymeric tubulin, staggered in such a manner that the tubulin monomers are arranged in a helical pattern on the microtubular surface, and with the alpha/beta axes of the tubulin subunits parallel to the long axis of the tubule; exist in equilibrium with pool of tubulin monomers and can be rapidly assembled or disassembled in response to physiological stimuli; concerned with force generation, e.g. in the spindle.

go_terms.name: chemical synaptic transmission
go_terms.definition: The vesicular release of classical neurotransmitter molecules from a presynapse, across a chemical synapse, the subsequent activation of neurotransmitter receptors at the postsynapse of a target cell (neuron, muscle, or secretory cell) and the effects of this activation on the postsynaptic membrane potential and ionic composition of the postsynaptic cytosol. This process encompasses both spontaneous and evoked release of neurotransmitter and all parts of synaptic vesicle exocytosis. Evoked transmission starts with the arrival of an action potential at the presynapse.

go_terms.name: substantia nigra development
go_terms.definition: The progression of the substantia nigra over time from its initial formation until its mature state. The substantia nigra is the layer of gray substance that separates the posterior parts of the cerebral peduncles (tegmentum mesencephali) from the anterior parts; it normally includes a posterior compact part with many pigmented cells (pars compacta) and an anterior reticular part whose cells contain little pigment (pars reticularis).

go_terms.name: myelin sheath
go_terms.definition: An electrically insulating fatty layer that surrounds the axons of many neurons. It is an outgrowth of glial cells: Schwann cells supply the myelin for peripheral neurons while oligodendrocytes supply it to those of the central nervous system.

go_terms.name: synapse
go_terms.definition: The junction between an axon of one neuron and a dendrite of another neuron, a muscle fiber or a glial cell. As the axon approaches the synapse it enlarges into a specialized structure, the presynaptic terminal bouton, which contains mitochondria and synaptic vesicles. At the tip of the terminal bouton is the presynaptic membrane; facing it, and separated from it by a minute cleft (the synaptic cleft) is a specialized area of membrane on the receiving cell, known as the postsynaptic membrane. In response to the arrival of nerve impulses, the presynaptic terminal bouton secretes molecules of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft. These diffuse across the cleft and transmit the signal to the postsynaptic membrane.

go_terms.name: extracellular exosome
go_terms.definition: A vesicle that is released into the extracellular region by fusion of the limiting endosomal membrane of a multivesicular body with the plasma membrane. Extracellular exosomes, also simply called exosomes, have a diameter of about 40-100 nm.

go_terms.name: endoplasmic reticulum
go_terms.definition: The irregular network of unit membranes, visible only by electron microscopy, that occurs in the cytoplasm of many eukaryotic cells. The membranes form a complex meshwork of tubular channels, which are often expanded into slitlike cavities called cisternae. The ER takes two forms, rough (or granular), with ribosomes adhering to the outer surface, and smooth (with no ribosomes attached).

go_terms.definition: A structure comprised of a core structure (in most organisms, a pair of centrioles) and peripheral material from which a microtubule-based structure, such as a spindle apparatus, is organized. Centrosomes occur close to the nucleus during interphase in many eukaryotic cells, though in animal cells it changes continually during the cell-division cycle.

go_terms.name: DNA repair
go_terms.definition: The process of restoring DNA after damage. Genomes are subject to damage by chemical and physical agents in the environment (e.g. UV and ionizing radiations, chemical mutagens, fungal and bacterial toxins, etc.) and by free radicals or alkylating agents endogenously generated in metabolism. DNA is also damaged because of errors during its replication. A variety of different DNA repair pathways have been reported that include direct reversal, base excision repair, nucleotide excision repair, photoreactivation, bypass, double-strand break repair pathway, and mismatch repair pathway.

go_terms.name: nucleolus
go_terms.definition: A small, dense body one or more of which are present in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. It is rich in RNA and protein, is not bounded by a limiting membrane, and is not seen during mitosis. Its prime function is the transcription of the nucleolar DNA into 45S ribosomal-precursor RNA, the processing of this RNA into 5.8S, 18S, and 28S components of ribosomal RNA, and the association of these components with 5S RNA and proteins synthesized outside the nucleolus. This association results in the formation of ribonucleoprotein precursors; these pass into the cytoplasm and mature into the 40S and 60S subunits of the ribosome.

ADPRHL1.functional_summary: ADPRHL1 exhibits ADP-ribosylarginine-[protein] hydrolase activity, catalyzing the removal of ADP-ribose from arginine residues on proteins, consistent with its role in protein de-ADP-ribosylation. It is implicated in cardiac-specific processes such as cardiac chamber ballooning and cardiac myofibril assembly, suggesting a function in heart morphogenesis and muscle structure formation. Localization to the sarcomere supports its involvement in the organization or maintenance of cardiac muscle contractile units.
ADPRHL1.expression_interpretation: ADPRHL1 shows higher expression in muscle-related tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in skeletal muscle and cardiac tissues such as the left ventricle and atrial appendage. Moderate expression is also detected in nerve and arterial tissues, though at notably lower levels compared to muscle. This pattern may suggest a functional role for ADPRHL1 in muscle and cardiovascular systems relative to other tissues measured.
ADPRHL1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of ADPRHL1 comprises nine interactions, highlighting a selective set of partners that may reflect its functional associations. Notably, interactions with proteins such as GRTP1 and DCUN1D2 suggest potential involvement in cellular processes related to protein modification and regulation. These interactions are supported with moderate to high confidence, underscoring the reliability of several key network connections.
ADPRHL1.gene_summary: ADPRHL1 encodes an ADP-ribosylhydrolase-like protein involved in protein de-ADP-ribosylation, cardiac chamber ballooning, and cardiac myofibril assembly. It has nine known interaction partners, including GRTP1, DCUN1D2, and TMCO3. Expression of ADPRHL1 is highest in skeletal muscle. Mutations in ADPRHL1 cause cardiac developmental defects characterized by impaired heart chamber growth and myofibrillogenesis, and there is also evidence linking germline variants in ADPRHL1 to increased prostate cancer risk through promotion of cell proliferation. The literature on ADPRHL1 spans themes including cardiac development and function, cancer risk and progression, and molecular regulation of actin assembly, with recent studies investigating ADP-ribosylation signaling pathways.

AKAP17A.expression_interpretation: AKAP17A shows higher expression in several tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in ovary, spleen, and thyroid among the tissues measured. Additionally, notable expression is present in the cervix endocervix and EBV-transformed lymphocytes, indicating enrichment in both reproductive and immune-related tissues. This pattern may suggest a role for AKAP17A in functions pertinent to these tissue types, although further investigation is needed to clarify its biological significance.

AKAP17A.gene_summary: AKAP17A encodes a protein with a currently unknown core molecular function or biological role. It has no experimentally validated interaction partners, with zero confirmed protein interactions reported. Expression of AKAP17A is highest in the ovary and spleen. Clinically, AKAP17A is relevant to cancer biology through its role in promoting hypoxic adaptation and tumor growth by enhancing HIF1α protein levels, and it is implicated in modulating chemotherapy response in ovarian cancer; additionally, its transcript levels in peripheral blood are predictive of cognitive decline and physical ageing phenotypes, suggesting involvement in age-related molecular processes. The literature on AKAP17A spans themes including RNA splicing regulation, hypoxic tumor adaptation, and ageing-associated splicing factors, with studies investigating its contribution to transposable element excision.

BHLHE23.functional_summary: BHLHE23 functions as a DNA-binding transcription factor that specifically binds to E-box motifs, modulating transcription by RNA polymerase II and positively regulating gene expression. It also exhibits protein dimerization activity, which may facilitate its role in sequence-specific double-stranded DNA binding. Localization of BHLHE23 to the nucleus and chromatin is consistent with its involvement in regulating transcriptional processes during sensory organ and axon development. Mechanistic detail beyond these functions is limited based on the provided annotations.
BHLHE23.expression_interpretation: BHLHE23 expression is highest within the GTEx dataset in testis, showing notably greater levels compared to other measured tissues. Expression in EBV-transformed lymphocytes, bladder, and heart atrial appendage is considerably lower, indicating enrichment in testis relative to these tissues. This pattern may suggest a tissue-specific role for BHLHE23 in testis or reflect limited expression in other tissues not included in this dataset.
BHLHE23.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of BHLHE23 comprises 18 interactions, prominently featuring partners involved in transcriptional regulation such as TCF3 and homeobox proteins VSX1 and VSX2. These interactions suggest a role for BHLHE23 in gene expression modulation, supported by moderate to high confidence in its associations with these key transcription factors. The presence of AP3S1 and AP3S2 indicates potential links to vesicular trafficking processes, although these connections are less characterized.
BHLHE23.gene_summary: BHLHE23 encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor involved in sensory organ development, positive regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II, and axon development. It has 18 known protein interactions, with top partners including AP3S2, AP3S1, TCF3, VSX1, and VSX2. Expression of BHLHE23 is highest in the testis. Although BHLHE23 has been noted in the context of evolutionary conservation and neurodevelopmental regulatory roles, there is no direct evidence establishing it as a causative gene for any specific clinical disorder or neurodevelopmental phenotype. BHLHE23 has limited dedicated literature. It has appeared as an incidental finding across studies of transcriptional regulation in neural progenitor cells, evolutionary conservation of gene regulation, and neurodevelopmental disorder mechanisms, but no papers in this set focus specifically on BHLHE23.

BMP3.functional_summary: BMP3 functions as a growth factor with cytokine activity that binds to BMP receptors, mediating cell-cell signaling through receptor interactions that likely influence downstream cellular processes. It plays a role in skeletal system development and osteoblast differentiation, as well as in the negative regulation of ossification, suggesting it modulates bone formation and remodeling. Localization of BMP3 to the extracellular region and extracellular exosomes is consistent with its role as a secreted signaling molecule involved in intercellular communication during tissue development. Mechanistic detail is limited to these functional annotations and interaction data.
BMP3.expression_interpretation: BMP3 shows higher expression in several gastrointestinal tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the sigmoid colon, followed by the transverse colon and terminal ileum. Additionally, notable expression is detected in the tibial nerve and esophagus muscularis, indicating a broader tissue distribution beyond the digestive tract. This pattern suggests that BMP3 may have functional relevance in both gastrointestinal and peripheral nervous system tissues among those measured.
BMP3.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of BMP3 encompasses 58 interactions, prominently featuring receptors such as ACVR2B and ACVR2A, which suggests a role in signaling processes related to the TGF-beta superfamily. Interactions with BMPR1B further support its involvement in receptor-mediated activities. These associations include several high-confidence interactions, underscoring the robustness of key identified interactions.
BMP3.gene_summary: BMP3 encodes bone morphogenetic protein 3, a key regulator of skeletal system development and osteoblast differentiation, functioning primarily to negatively regulate ossification through serine/threonine kinase signaling pathways. It engages with a network of 58 interaction partners, most notably ACVR2B, NDRG4, AMBN, ACVR2A, and BMPR1B. Expression of BMP3 is highest in the colon—sigmoid. Although specific clinical conditions linked to BMP3 are not detailed in the source data, the gene plays an influential role in osteogenic differentiation and bone density modulation, implicating its importance in bone formation and skeletal health. The literature on BMP3 spans themes including the regulation of osteogenic differentiation, BMP3 gene expression control, and bone density modulation, with studies investigating the molecular pathways that govern osteogenesis and skeletal development.

CNP.functional_summary: CNP catalyzes the hydrolysis of nucleoside 2',3'-cyclic phosphate to nucleoside 2'-phosphate, indicating a role in the cyclic nucleotide catabolic process. It is also involved in chemical synaptic transmission, which encompasses the vesicular release of neurotransmitters and subsequent activation of postsynaptic receptors. Localization to the cytoplasm and mitochondrion is consistent with functions related to intracellular signaling and energy metabolism, while presence in the extracellular region may suggest additional roles in the cellular environment. Mechanistic detail beyond these annotations is limited.
CNP.expression_interpretation: CNP expression is enriched in nervous system tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the spinal cord (cervical c-1), followed by peripheral nerve and several brain regions including the substantia nigra, hippocampus, and putamen. This pattern suggests a prominent role for CNP in neural tissues relative to others measured. The notably elevated expression in the spinal cord may indicate a particular functional importance in this region compared to other nervous system sites.
CNP.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network for CNP reveals a focused set of associations predominantly involving key myelin-related proteins, suggesting a role in oligodendrocyte function and myelin sheath maintenance. Notably, interactions with MBP, GFAP, and MAG are observed with generally high confidence, underscoring their potential biological relevance. These connections highlight CNP's integration within a specialized cellular context rather than broad, nonspecific interactions.
CNP.gene_summary: CNP encodes a 2',3'-cyclic nucleotide 3' phosphodiesterase involved in cyclic nucleotide catabolic processes and chemical synaptic transmission. It has 105 known interaction partners, with top partners including MBP, GFAP, MAG, PLP1, and OLIG2; CNP is annotated to the extracellular region, cytoplasm, and mitochondrion. Expression of CNP is highest in the brain, specifically the cervical spinal cord. Clinically, altered CNP expression is linked to disorders affecting oligodendrocyte function and myelin integrity, such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and effects from perinatal methadone or ethanol exposure, which impact myelin protein regulation and contribute to neurodegeneration. The literature on CNP spans themes including myelin and oligodendrogenesis, neural progenitor cell regulation, and natriuretic peptide expression, with studies investigating its role in pain signaling pathways and cardiovascular and renal function.

COL11A1.functional_summary: COL11A1 functions as an extracellular matrix structural constituent that contributes to the organization and tensile strength of collagen fibrils, thereby maintaining the structural integrity of the extracellular matrix. It also exhibits extracellular matrix binding and protein-macromolecule adaptor activities, facilitating coordinated interactions among matrix components. Localization of COL11A1 to collagen type XI trimers within the extracellular region is consistent with a role in skeletal system morphogenesis and collagen fibril organization. Mechanistic detail beyond these functions is limited based on the provided annotations.
COL11A1.expression_interpretation: COL11A1 shows highest expression within the GTEx dataset in cultured fibroblasts, with notably lower but appreciable levels observed in testis, tibial nerve, hypothalamus, and pituitary tissues. This pattern indicates that COL11A1 expression is enriched in connective tissue-related cells and certain neural and endocrine tissues relative to others measured. The distribution may suggest diverse roles across these tissue types, although expression in tissues not included in the dataset cannot be excluded.
COL11A1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of COL11A1 reveals extensive connectivity predominantly with other collagen family members, indicating its integral role in extracellular matrix organization. The interactions with key partners such as COL1A2 and COL5A2 occur with generally high confidence, underscoring the robustness of these associations. This network highlights the structural interplay critical for maintaining tissue integrity.
COL11A1.gene_summary: COL11A1 encodes the alpha 1 chain of type XI collagen, a minor fibrillar collagen involved in the organization of collagen fibrils and contributing to skeletal system morphogenesis and sensory perception processes. It interacts with 158 proteins, most notably COL1A2, COL5A2, COL2A1, COL1A1, and COL3A1. Expression of COL11A1 is highest in cultured fibroblasts. Clinically, COL11A1 is strongly implicated in disorders affecting connective tissues, including ocular and craniofacial abnormalities, as well as genetic hearing loss, reflecting its key role in extracellular matrix structure and development. The literature on COL11A1 spans themes including genetic hearing loss, cancer progression mechanisms, and extracellular matrix organization, with recent studies investigating its role in fibrosis and tumor biology.

DHRSX.functional_summary: [LOW_EVIDENCE] Insufficient annotation data to generate experimental relevance context for DHRSX.
DHRSX.expression_interpretation: DHRSX shows higher expression in the cervix, including both endocervix and ectocervix, as well as in cultured fibroblasts, thyroid, and prostate tissues among those measured in the GTEx dataset. These tissues represent the highest expression levels within the dataset, indicating an enrichment of DHRSX expression in these specific tissue types relative to others measured. Expression in other tissues is comparatively lower, suggesting a tissue-enriched pattern rather than widespread high expression across all GTEx tissues.
DHRSX.interaction_interpretation: [LOW_EVIDENCE] No protein interactions are recorded for DHRSX in STRING.
DHRSX.gene_summary: DHRSX encodes an enzyme essential for dolichol biosynthesis, catalyzing key steps in this multi-stage pathway. It has no reported protein interaction partners, with no interactions found to date. Expression of DHRSX is highest in cervix - endocervix tissue. Mutations in DHRSX cause a pseudoautosomal-recessive congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by defects in N-glycosylation, contributing to a spectrum of clinical presentations involving impaired glycosylation pathways. The literature on DHRSX spans themes including dolichol biosynthesis defects, N-glycosylation disorders, and autophagy regulation, with studies investigating its role as a non-classical secretory protein and its involvement in neurodevelopmental disorders.

DMRTA2.functional_summary: DMRTA2 functions as a sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factor that modulates transcription mediated by RNA polymerase II, indicating a role in regulating gene expression. It is involved in the biological process of sex differentiation, suggesting it contributes to the establishment of organismal sex through physical differentiation. Localization to the nucleus and association with chromatin are consistent with its role in regulating DNA-templated transcription by interacting with specific cis-regulatory DNA sequences.
DMRTA2.expression_interpretation: DMRTA2 expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in testis, followed by notable expression in the pituitary and esophageal mucosa. Lower but detectable expression is present in certain brain regions, including the spinal cord and cerebellum, while other tissues show comparatively reduced levels. This pattern may suggest tissue-specific roles for DMRTA2, particularly in reproductive and neuroendocrine contexts, although further investigation is needed to clarify its functional significance.
DMRTA2.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of DMRTA2 comprises 11 interactions, prominently featuring partners involved in transcriptional regulation such as EMX2 and NFIA. These interactions suggest a role for DMRTA2 in gene expression modulation, supported by low to moderate confidence in some associations. The network highlights DMRTA2's potential involvement in developmental processes without indicating specific pathway or complex membership.
DMRTA2.gene_summary: DMRTA2 encodes a transcription factor involved in the regulation of DNA-templated transcription and sex differentiation. It engages with 11 interaction partners, prominently including EMX2, NFIA, and FOXL1, and is annotated to chromatin within the nucleus. Expression of DMRTA2 is highest in the testis. Clinically, DMRTA2 is strongly linked to neural progenitor cell maintenance defects and cortical development abnormalities, with implications in pediatric gliomas where its dysregulation impacts tumorigenicity and neovascularization. The literature on DMRTA2 spans themes including neural progenitor maintenance, cortical development regulation, and glioma tumorigenicity, with recent studies investigating its roles in transcriptional and epigenetic regulation as well as sex differentiation and germ cell development.

EBF2.functional_summary: EBF2 functions as a DNA-binding transcription factor that specifically interacts with cis-regulatory regions recognized by RNA polymerase II, thereby positively regulating transcription from these promoters. It modulates the frequency and rate of RNA polymerase II-mediated transcription, including activation of gene expression in response to cold-induced thermogenesis. Localization of EBF2 to the nucleus and its association with chromatin are consistent with a role in regulating DNA-templated transcription through direct interaction with chromosomal DNA.
EBF2.expression_interpretation: EBF2 expression is highest within the GTEx dataset in nerve tissue, specifically the tibial nerve, with notably elevated levels compared to other tissues measured. Additionally, adipose tissues, both subcutaneous and visceral, show relatively high expression, followed by moderate expression in thyroid and breast mammary tissue. This pattern suggests that EBF2 may have functional relevance in peripheral nerve and adipose tissues among those captured by GTEx.
EBF2.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of EBF2 comprises 39 interactions, highlighting its connectivity with key regulatory proteins such as ZNF423 and PRDM16. These interactions suggest a role in transcriptional regulation and cellular differentiation, supported by generally high confidence in several top partners. The presence of factors like PPARG further underscores EBF2's involvement in metabolic and developmental processes.
EBF2.gene_summary: EBF2 encodes a transcription factor that regulates DNA-templated transcription and positively modulates transcription by RNA polymerase II, contributing to processes such as cold-induced thermogenesis. It interacts with 39 partners, most notably ZNF423, TMTC1, PRDM16, PPARG, and ID1, and is annotated to localize within chromatin and the nucleus. Expression of EBF2 is highest in tibial nerve tissue. EBF2 disruption causes adipose fibrosis and dysfunction leading to atypical partial lipodystrophy, characterized by impaired adipocyte differentiation and altered mitochondrial gene expression, and it also functions as a tumor suppressor by inhibiting pancreatic cancer progression and influencing osteosarcoma apoptosis. The literature on EBF2 spans themes including neurodevelopment and neuronal function, adipocyte differentiation and metabolism, and cancer biology and tumor suppression, with studies examining the gene’s role in bone development and osteogenesis.

EMX1.functional_summary: EMX1 functions as a sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factor that modulates transcription mediated by RNA polymerase II, thereby regulating DNA-templated transcription. It is involved in biological processes related to central nervous system and brain development, as well as neuron differentiation, indicating a role in neural maturation. Localization of EMX1 to the nucleus and chromatin is consistent with its function in regulating gene expression at the level of chromosomal DNA.
EMX1.expression_interpretation: EMX1 expression is enriched in kidney tissues within the GTEx dataset, showing the highest levels in both the cortex and medulla regions. Additionally, several brain regions, including the frontal cortex, general cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex, exhibit moderate expression relative to other tissues measured. This pattern may suggest a functional role for EMX1 in both renal and specific neural contexts captured by the dataset.
EMX1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of EMX1 encompasses 65 interactions, prominently featuring partners involved in neurodevelopmental processes such as TBR1 and FOXG1. These interactions suggest a role for EMX1 in transcriptional regulation during brain development, supported by generally high confidence in key associations. The presence of multiple neurogenic factors among its top partners underscores EMX1's functional relevance in neuronal differentiation.
EMX1.gene_summary: EMX1 encodes a homeobox transcription factor critical for regulating DNA-templated transcription and central nervous system development, including brain development and neuron differentiation. It interacts with 65 partners, notably TBR1, FOXG1, NEUROD6, SHH, and BCL11B, and is annotated to chromatin, nucleus, and nucleolus. Expression is highest in the kidney cortex and medulla. Clinical findings emphasize EMX1’s role in tumor suppression, where its downregulation correlates with malignancy and stemness in cancers such as spinal cord glioma and sarcomas, indicating its importance in modulating cell differentiation and tumorigenic properties. The literature on EMX1 spans themes including neural progenitor maintenance, transcriptional regulation, and brain development, with studies investigating its role in Wnt signaling pathway modulation and cancer suppression mechanisms.

EOMES.functional_summary: EOMES functions as a sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factor that modulates the transcription of genes transcribed by RNA polymerase II, likely through interaction with cis-regulatory regions. It is involved in biological processes such as endoderm and mesoderm formation, as well as endodermal cell fate specification, indicating a role in early developmental patterning. Localization of EOMES to the nucleus and chromatin is consistent with its function in regulating gene expression at the level of chromatin-bound DNA.
EOMES.expression_interpretation: EOMES expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellum among brain regions measured. Moderate expression is also detected in the spleen, while lower but detectable levels are present in whole blood and lung tissues. This pattern may suggest a role for EOMES in certain neural and immune-related tissues captured by the dataset.
EOMES.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of EOMES encompasses 287 interactions, highlighting its involvement with key transcription factors and immune-related proteins such as CD8A and TBXT. These interactions suggest a role in transcriptional regulation and immune cell function, supported by generally high confidence in several top partner associations. The network complexity underscores EOMES's multifaceted regulatory potential without implying specific pathway memberships.
EOMES.gene_summary: EOMES encodes eomesodermin, a T-box transcription factor that is fundamental for the regulation of neurogenesis, endoderm and mesoderm formation, as well as neuron migration. It coordinates with 287 interaction partners, most notably CD8A, TBXT, SMAD2, GZMK, and MIXL1. Expression of EOMES is highest in the brain, specifically the cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellum. The gene is critically involved in neurodevelopmental processes where disruptions affect cortical development, intermediate progenitor function, and neural circuit organization, contributing to brain structural abnormalities and intellectual disability phenotypes observed in related conditions. The literature on EOMES spans themes including neurogenesis regulation, cortical development, and transcriptional control mechanisms, with recent studies investigating its role in intermediate progenitor function and brain structural abnormalities.

F8A1.functional_summary: F8A1 is implicated in endosomal transport and vesicle cytoskeletal trafficking, indicating a role in the directed movement of substances via endosomes along cytoskeletal fibers. It also participates in protein binding and negatively regulates proteasomal protein catabolic processes, suggesting involvement in modulating protein degradation. Localization to the early endosome and cytoplasm is consistent with a function in intracellular trafficking and cargo sorting within the endosomal system.
F8A1.expression_interpretation: [LOW_EVIDENCE] No expression data available for F8A1 in GTEx.
F8A1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of F8A1 reveals a focused set of associations, prominently including HTT and F8, suggesting potential functional relevance in coagulation or related biological processes. These interactions include several with high confidence, indicating evidence for biological significance, though some partners have moderate to lower confidence scores. The presence of closely related family members F8A2 and F8A3 further underscores a conserved interaction pattern within this protein group.
F8A1.gene_summary: F8A1 encodes a protein involved in coagulation factor VIII-associated functions, playing roles in processes such as endosomal transport, vesicle cytoskeletal trafficking, and negative regulation of proteasomal protein catabolic process. It interacts with nine proteins in total, with top partners including HTT, F8, F8A2, F8A3, and ECEL1. The protein is annotated to localize in the nucleus, cytoplasm, and early endosome. Clinically, F8A1 is causally linked to severe Hemophilia A through genetic mechanisms including gene inversions, and genetic variation in F8A1 expression on the X-chromosome has also been associated with type 1 diabetes risk variants; additionally, its interaction with huntingtin protein implicates it in Huntington’s disease pathology related to vesicle transport and exocytosis. The literature on F8A1 spans themes including protein-protein interactions, X-chromosome genetic variation, and hemophilia A genetic mechanisms, with studies investigating antibody development for diagnostic purposes.

F8A2.functional_summary: No GO annotations are currently recorded in the Gene Ontology database for this gene. Functional characterisation cannot be determined from annotation data alone.
F8A2.expression_interpretation: [LOW_EVIDENCE] No expression data available for F8A2 in GTEx.
F8A2.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of F8A2 reveals a focused set of interactions predominantly involving proteins associated with intracellular trafficking and vesicular transport, including HTT and RAB5A. The presence of closely related family members F8A1 and F8A3 suggests potential functional or regulatory relationships within this protein family. These interactions include several with high confidence scores, underscoring the robustness of key observed associations.
F8A2.gene_summary: F8A2 encodes the coagulation factor VIII associated 2 protein, which is involved in cellular processes linked to endosome movement and gene inversion events. It interacts with 10 partners, most notably HTT, RAB5A, F8A1, F8A3, and HAP1. Expression data for F8A2 are not available to determine the highest-expressed tissue. Clinically, F8A2 is implicated in genetic mutations underlying severe Hemophilia A and is used in assays to detect gene inversions related to this X-linked bleeding disorder, highlighting its role in coagulation defects. The literature on F8A2 spans themes including gene expression variation and genetic mutations in hemophilia; immune system regulation and transcriptional regulation in neural progenitor cells are linked to broader gene sets rather than specifically to F8A2.

F8A3.functional_summary: No GO annotations are currently recorded in the Gene Ontology database for this gene. Functional characterisation cannot be determined from annotation data alone.
F8A3.expression_interpretation: F8A3 expression is consistently low across the tissues measured in the GTEx dataset, with little variation observed among the 54 tissue types analyzed. The gene shows slightly higher expression in thyroid, arterial tissues, tibial nerve, and endocervical cervix relative to other tissues measured, though these differences are modest and do not indicate strong tissue specificity. This pattern suggests that F8A3 may have low overall expression or may be more prominently expressed in tissues not included in the GTEx dataset.
F8A3.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of F8A3 comprises a limited number of partners, including notable associations with HTT and closely related F8A family members, suggesting potential functional or evolutionary relationships within this group. The interactions include moderate to high confidence scores (ranging approximately from 0.42 to 0.95), indicating overall credible but variable support. This network highlights F8A3's involvement in a specific subset of protein interactions without broader connectivity to diverse cellular components.
F8A3.gene_summary: F8A3 encodes a protein associated with coagulation factor VIII, suggesting a role related to hemostasis or coagulation pathways. It engages with six interaction partners, notably including HTT, F8A1, F8A2, H2AB3, and ANKRD24. Expression of F8A3 is highest in the thyroid tissue. Clinically, F8A3 is involved in severe Hemophilia A through gene inversions detectable by specific PCR assays, and it has also been observed as differentially expressed in neural progenitor cells and neurons in Rett syndrome, indicating a potential connection to neurodevelopmental pathways. The literature on F8A3 has been studied in the context of X chromosome gene regulation, neurodevelopmental disorder pathways, and hemophilia A genetic mechanisms, with recent studies investigating transcriptional regulation in neural progenitor cells.

GREM2.functional_summary: GREM2 functions as a protein that binds bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) and acts as a protein sequestering agent, thereby negatively regulating the BMP signaling pathway. It also exhibits receptor ligand activity and heparin binding, suggesting it modulates signaling events through extracellular interactions. Localization to the extracellular region is consistent with a role in modulating signaling molecules outside the cell, influencing processes such as embryonic body morphogenesis and determination of dorsal identity. Mechanistic detail is limited to these binding and regulatory activities based on the provided annotations.
GREM2.expression_interpretation: GREM2 expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the colon, particularly the sigmoid and transverse regions, as well as the terminal ileum of the small intestine. Moderate expression is also noted in the liver and cultured fibroblasts relative to other tissues measured. This pattern may suggest a role for GREM2 in gastrointestinal and connective tissue contexts, although further investigation is needed to clarify its biological significance.
GREM2.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of GREM2 is characterized by its association with several bone morphogenetic proteins, including BMP2, BMP4, and BMP7, as well as its paralog GREM1, indicating a role in modulating signaling related to these ligands. These interactions are supported with generally high confidence, underscoring the relevance of GREM2 in contexts involving BMP family members.
GREM2.gene_summary: GREM2 encodes a DAN family protein that functions primarily as a bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) antagonist, playing a crucial role in regulating embryonic development and cytokine-mediated signaling. It interacts with 29 proteins, prominently BMP2, BMP4, BMP7, GREM1, and BMP6, and is annotated to the extracellular region. Expression of GREM2 is highest in the sigmoid colon. Clinically, GREM2 is implicated in metabolic disorders including type 2 diabetes through its association with β-cell function, as well as in central obesity by inhibiting the browning of visceral preadipocytes; it also has a role in neurological conditions such as seizure susceptibility and anxiety via its regulation of hippocampal neurogenesis and neural progenitor cell function. The literature on GREM2 spans themes including BMP signaling regulation, cardiac development and function, craniofacial and dental anomalies, metabolic regulation and obesity, neurogenesis, and neurological disorders, with recent studies investigating its role in metabolic regulation and neural function.

GYG2.functional_summary: GYG2 functions as a glycosyltransferase catalyzing the transfer of glucose residues from UDP-glucose to glycogenin, initiating glycogen biosynthesis through self-glucosylation and subsequent elongation of glucosyl chains. This enzymatic activity underlies its role in the glycogen biosynthetic process, facilitating the formation of branched glucose polymers. Localization of GYG2 to the cytosol and cytoplasm is consistent with its involvement in carbohydrate metabolism within the cellular milieu.
GYG2.expression_interpretation: GYG2 shows higher expression in adipose tissues, with subcutaneous and visceral adipose among the highest within the GTEx dataset, followed by moderate expression in mammary tissue and certain brain regions such as the spinal cord and substantia nigra. This pattern suggests that GYG2 expression is enriched in adipose tissues relative to others measured, with notable but lower expression in select neural and breast tissues. The distribution may suggest tissue-specific roles, particularly related to adipose function, though further investigation would be required to clarify biological implications.
GYG2.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of GYG2 reveals a focused set of interactions predominantly with proteins involved in glycogen metabolism, including GYS1, GYS2, and GYG1, suggesting a role in glycogen synthesis regulation. The interactions with GBE1 and AGL further support its involvement in carbohydrate processing, with several connections established with generally high confidence. This network underscores GYG2's functional association within a metabolic context without extending to broader pathway claims.
GYG2.gene_summary: GYG2 encodes glycogenin 2, a glycogenin protein that initiates glycogen biosynthesis by autoglucosylation, playing a key role in glycogen formation and glucose homeostasis. It has 69 reported interaction partners, including the glycogen synthase isoforms GYS1 and GYS2, glycogenin 1 (GYG1), glycogen branching enzyme (GBE1), and amylo-1,6-glucosidase (AGL). The highest expression of GYG2 is observed in subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue. Variants in GYG2 have been linked to altered glycogen metabolism and compensatory effects in glycogenin 1 deficiency, impacting glycogen synthase activity and energy homeostasis, with broader implications in metabolic regulation and aging biomarkers. The literature on GYG2 spans themes including glycogen metabolism regulation, genetic mutations and disease, and epigenetic and transcriptional control, with recent studies investigating its enzymatic activity and roles in cancer biology.

HSD17B7P2.gene_summary: HSD17B7P2 encodes a protein of unknown function without assigned biological processes. It has no reported interaction partners, indicating a total of zero known protein interactions. Expression data are not available for any specific human tissue. Clinically, HSD17B7P2 has been identified through multivariate genetic association studies as a gene with significant hits related to Alzheimer's disease subcortical imaging phenotypes, though no direct causal links or phenotypic spectra have been established. HSD17B7P2 has limited dedicated literature; it has appeared as an incidental finding across studies of neurodevelopmental disorders, transcriptional regulation, and neural progenitor cell biology, but no papers in this set focus specifically on HSD17B7P2.

LHX5.functional_summary: LHX5 functions as a DNA-binding transcription factor that specifically interacts with RNA polymerase II regulatory regions to modulate transcription. It is involved in the regulation and positive regulation of DNA-templated transcription, contributing to neuron differentiation, including the specialization of spinal cord association neurons. Localization of LHX5 to the nucleus and chromatin is consistent with its role in controlling gene expression at the level of chromatin-associated DNA. Mechanistic detail beyond transcriptional regulation and neuronal differentiation is limited based on the available GO annotations.
LHX5.expression_interpretation: LHX5 expression is enriched in specific brain regions within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the cerebellum, hypothalamus, and cerebellar hemisphere. Moderate expression is also detected in the stomach, while other tissues, including the substantia nigra, show comparatively lower levels. This pattern may suggest a role for LHX5 in certain neural and gastrointestinal contexts among the tissues measured.
LHX5.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of LHX5 reveals a focused set of interactions predominantly involving transcriptional regulators and developmental proteins, suggesting its role in neural development. Notably, interactions with partners such as CCNK and LDB1 occur with generally high confidence, underscoring their potential functional relevance. This network highlights LHX5's integration within a regulatory framework critical for gene expression modulation.
LHX5.gene_summary: LHX5 encodes a LIM homeobox transcription factor that regulates DNA-templated transcription and plays a key role in neuronal differentiation and spinal cord association neuron differentiation. It has 50 reported interaction partners, including prominent ones such as CCNK, BARHL1, ZIC1, DBX1, and LDB1; LHX5 is annotated to chromatin and the nucleus. Expression of LHX5 is highest in the brain, specifically in the cerebellum and hypothalamus. The clinical relevance of LHX5 encompasses its critical involvement in forebrain development and neuronal differentiation, with implications for neurodevelopmental processes affecting neuronal identity and dendritic morphogenesis, although direct disease causation is not explicitly defined in the available literature. The literature on LHX5 spans themes including LIM-homeodomain gene regulation, axon guidance and morphogenesis, and transcriptional control mechanisms, with studies particularly investigating its role in forebrain development and neuronal differentiation.

LHX9.functional_summary: LHX9 functions as a sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factor that modulates transcription mediated by RNA polymerase II, thereby regulating DNA-templated transcription. It is involved in biological processes such as neuron differentiation and dorsal spinal cord interneuron anterior axon guidance, indicating a role in neural development. Localization of LHX9 to the nucleus and chromatin is consistent with its function in regulating gene expression at the level of chromatin-associated DNA. Mechanistic detail beyond these activities is limited based on the provided annotations.
LHX9.expression_interpretation: LHX9 expression is highest within the GTEx dataset in ovarian tissue, with notably lower levels observed in testis and several vascular tissues, including coronary and tibial arteries. Expression in brain regions such as the hypothalamus is detectable but comparatively low relative to these tissues. This pattern suggests that LHX9 may have a more prominent role in reproductive and vascular tissues among those measured, although expression in other unmeasured tissues cannot be excluded.
LHX9.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of LHX9 encompasses 72 interactions, prominently featuring partners such as LDB1 and SSBP3, which suggest a role in transcriptional regulation. The presence of multiple LIM homeobox proteins among its top interactors indicates functional associations within this protein family. These interactions are supported with generally high confidence, underscoring their potential biological relevance.
LHX9.gene_summary: LHX9 encodes a LIM homeobox transcription factor involved in regulating DNA-templated transcription and neuron differentiation. It interacts with 72 partners, including key regulators such as LDB1, SSBP3, LHX2, POU4F1, and SSBP4. Expression of LHX9 is highest in the ovary. Clinically, LHX9 plays a critical role in brain and pineal gland development, with deletion causing hypoplastic pineal gland and hydrocephalus, and it is implicated in inflammatory conditions like endometriosis and cancer progression through metabolic reprogramming. The literature on LHX9 spans themes including neural development regulation, transcriptional control mechanisms, and cancer metabolic reprogramming, with recent studies investigating inflammatory response modulation.

LINC00839.functional_summary: [LOW_EVIDENCE] Insufficient annotation data to generate experimental relevance context for LINC00839.
LINC00839.expression_interpretation: LINC00839 shows higher expression in kidney cortex relative to other tissues measured within the GTEx dataset, with notable enrichment also observed in spleen and several brain regions including the caudate, frontal cortex, and nucleus accumbens. This pattern suggests that LINC00839 may have functional relevance in both renal and specific neural tissues, although its expression is not exclusive to a single tissue type. The observed distribution may suggest diverse roles across these systems, warranting further investigation.

LINC00839.gene_summary: LINC00839 encodes a long intergenic non-protein coding RNA that literature suggests has roles in gene regulation. It has no reported protein interaction partners, with zero interactions identified in available datasets. Expression of LINC00839 is highest in kidney cortex tissue. Clinically, LINC00839 is implicated in cancer progression, particularly lung adenocarcinoma, oral squamous cell carcinoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, where it contributes to tumor growth, metastasis, and may have diagnostic value. The literature on LINC00839 spans themes including cancer progression mechanisms, lncRNA-miRNA interactions, and signaling pathway regulation, with recent studies investigating its role in therapy resistance and tumor microenvironment modulation.

LINC02688.functional_summary: [LOW_EVIDENCE] Insufficient annotation data to generate experimental relevance context for LINC02688.
LINC02688.expression_interpretation: LINC02688 shows highest expression within the GTEx dataset in the spleen, with notably lower levels observed in brain regions such as the nucleus accumbens and cerebellum, as well as in testis and the terminal ileum of the small intestine. This pattern indicates that LINC02688 is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, particularly the spleen, relative to other measured tissues. The elevated expression in these diverse tissues may suggest distinct regulatory roles or functions that warrant further investigation.
LINC02688.interaction_interpretation: [LOW_EVIDENCE] No protein interactions are recorded for LINC02688 in STRING.
LINC02688.gene_summary: LINC02688 encodes a long intergenic non-protein coding RNA with no currently annotated biological processes. It has no known interaction partners, with interaction data indicating zero proteins linked to LINC02688. Expression of LINC02688 is highest in the spleen. Clinically, LINC02688 has been identified as one of several necroptosis-related lncRNAs implicated in forming a prognostic risk score model for cervical squamous cell carcinoma and endocervical adenocarcinoma, suggesting a role in cancer prognosis and immune response modulation. The literature on LINC02688 has been studied mainly in the context of lncRNA involvement in cancer prognosis, immune response regulation, and necroptosis mechanisms; claims about transcriptional regulation in neural progenitor cells pertain to related gene sets but not directly to LINC02688.

MED12.functional_summary: MED12 functions as a transcription coregulator that modulates the transcription of specific gene sets by interacting with DNA-binding transcription factors, often altering chromatin structure or facilitating interactions with other coregulators. It exhibits sequence-specific DNA binding to RNA polymerase II cis-regulatory regions and promotes positive regulation of transcription initiation by RNA polymerase II. Localization of MED12 to the nucleoplasm within the nucleus is consistent with its role in regulating transcriptional processes at chromatin sites.
MED12.expression_interpretation: MED12 shows higher expression in reproductive tissues such as the ovary, uterus, and cervix (both endocervix and ectocervix) relative to other tissues measured within the GTEx dataset. Additionally, notable expression is observed in nerve - tibial, indicating that MED12 may have functional relevance in both reproductive and nervous system tissues. This pattern suggests that MED12 expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset rather than being uniformly distributed.
MED12.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of MED12 encompasses 183 interactions, prominently featuring associations with MED13, MED6, and MED24 among others. These interactions suggest a central role for MED12 within a tightly connected group of proteins, supported by generally high confidence in the top partners. The network topology highlights MED12 as a key node potentially coordinating multiple protein interactions.
MED12.gene_summary: MED12 encodes a core subunit of the Mediator complex that plays a critical role in the regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II. It coordinates with 183 interaction partners, including key Mediator components MED13, MED6, and MED24; MED12 is annotated to the nucleoplasm. Expression of MED12 is highest in the ovary and uterus. MED12 causes a spectrum of developmental disorders characterized primarily by intellectual disability, such as MED12-related intellectual disability syndromes and Lujan-Fryns syndrome, and is also implicated in congenital diaphragmatic hernia seen in Hardikar syndrome, with phenotypes expanding to include epilepsy without intellectual disability. The literature on MED12 spans themes including Mediator complex transcriptional regulation, the clinical and phenotypic spectrum of MED12-related disorders, and MED12 signaling pathway dysregulation, with recent studies investigating the expanding clinical manifestations of MED12 mutations.

NDST4.functional_summary: NDST4 exhibits sulfotransferase activity, specifically catalyzing the transfer of sulfate groups to heparan sulfate chains, thereby modifying alpha-D-glucosaminyl residues through N-sulfation. This enzymatic function contributes to the biosynthetic processes of heparan sulfate and heparin proteoglycans, which involve the formation of sulfated glycosaminoglycan chains linked to core proteins. Localization of NDST4 to the Golgi apparatus and its membrane is consistent with a role in the post-translational modification and processing of proteoglycans within the secretory pathway.
NDST4.expression_interpretation: NDST4 expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in nerve (tibial), prostate, ovary, and testis among the tissues measured. Moderate expression is also noted in the spleen, while other tissues exhibit comparatively lower levels. This pattern may suggest a role for NDST4 in these reproductive and nervous system-related tissues, although further investigation is needed to clarify its functional significance.
NDST4.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of NDST4 encompasses 39 interactions, prominently featuring partners involved in heparan sulfate biosynthesis and modification. These associations suggest a functional role for NDST4 in glycosaminoglycan metabolism, supported by interactions with enzymes and proteoglycans such as HS2ST1 and members of the glypican family. The network is characterized by generally moderate confidence interactions, underscoring the reliability of these functional connections.
NDST4.gene_summary: NDST4 encodes an enzyme with N-deacetylase and N-sulfotransferase activities that participates in the biosynthesis of heparan sulfate proteoglycans. It engages in 39 protein interactions, prominently with HS2ST1, GLCE, GPC5, GPC3, and GPC2. Expression of NDST4 is highest in nerve tissue, specifically the tibial nerve. Clinically, NDST4 functions as a tumor suppressor gene with marked downregulation and allelic loss observed in colorectal cancer, where its deficiency also affects colonic epithelial cell differentiation, indicating a role in colonic epithelial homeostasis. The literature on NDST4 spans themes including heparan sulfate biosynthesis, cancer tumor suppression, and enzyme structure and function, with recent studies investigating genetic association and gene expression regulation.

NHLH1.functional_summary: NHLH1 functions as a DNA-binding transcription factor that specifically interacts with RNA polymerase II regulatory regions to modulate transcription, including activating gene expression. It is involved in the positive regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II and plays a role in central nervous system development. Localization of NHLH1 to the nucleus and chromatin is consistent with its role in regulating gene expression at the level of chromosomal DNA.
NHLH1.expression_interpretation: NHLH1 expression is enriched in specific brain regions within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in basal ganglia structures such as the caudate, nucleus accumbens, and putamen, as well as in the cerebellum and cerebellar hemisphere. Relative to other tissues measured, these brain areas show notably higher expression, suggesting a potential role for NHLH1 in neural contexts. Expression in non-brain tissues is comparatively lower, which may indicate either low overall expression or activity in tissues not included in the GTEx dataset.
NHLH1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of NHLH1 comprises 36 interactions, highlighting its connectivity with several transcription factors involved in neural development. Notably, interactions with LHX9, NEUROD1, and NEUROD2 suggest a role in neuronal differentiation processes. These associations are supported with moderate to high confidence, underscoring the relevance of NHLH1 within this regulatory context.
NHLH1.gene_summary: NHLH1 encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that regulates transcription by RNA polymerase II and is involved in central nervous system development. Clinical findings highlight NHLH1’s role in neurogenesis and neuronal differentiation, with functional importance for midbrain dopaminergic neuron development, although direct inherited disease causality is not explicitly stated. The literature on NHLH1 spans themes including neurogenesis regulation, transcriptional network mapping, and neuronal differentiation mechanisms, with recent studies investigating its role in transcription factor networks and disease-associated gene expression.

PCDHA3.gene_summary: PCDHA3 encodes protocadherin alpha 3, a protein involved in mediating cell adhesion and homophilic cell-cell adhesion critical for nervous system development. The literature on PCDHA3 spans themes including cancer metastasis inhibition, neuropsychiatric disorder genetics, and cadherin gene cluster variation, with recent studies investigating gene regulation by noncoding RNA and epithelial-mesenchymal transition.

PCDHA5.gene_summary: PCDHA5 encodes protocadherin alpha 5, a protein that mediates cell adhesion and plays a role in nervous system development through homophilic cell-cell adhesion. The role of PCDHA5 in neurological and oncological contexts remains underexplored, but it has been studied in the context of neural development regulation, gene expression modulation, and cancer biomarker identification.

PCDHB5.gene_summary: PCDHB5 encodes protocadherin beta 5, a protein involved in cell adhesion, homophilic cell-cell adhesion, nervous system development, synapse assembly, and chemical synaptic transmission. PCDHGA3.gene_summary: PCDHGA3 encodes a member of the protocadherin gamma subfamily A, which mediates homophilic cell-cell adhesion and contributes to nervous system development. It has 11 known protein interactions, with top partners including PCDHGA2, PCDHGA4, PCDHGA11, PCDHGA9, and PCDHGC3. Expression of PCDHGA3 is highest in the ovary. PREX1.functional_summary: PREX1 functions as a guanyl-nucleotide exchange factor that stimulates the exchange of GDP for GTP on signaling GTPases, thereby activating them. It is involved in the positive regulation of cell migration and modulates actin filament polymerization, processes essential for cellular motility. Mechanistic detail beyond these activities is limited based on the provided annotations.

PREX1.gene_summary: PREX1 encodes a phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate dependent Rac exchange factor that regulates actin filament polymerization and positive cell migration. It has 66 known interaction partners, with the top partners including RAC3, RAC1, GNB1, CDC42, and GNG2. Expression of PREX1 is highest in whole blood. Additionally, PREX1 activity influences glucose homeostasis and has relevance in cancer progression through mechanisms that affect cell motility and metastasis. The literature on PREX1 spans themes including cancer progression mechanisms, immune cell regulation, and metabolic regulation, with recent studies investigating protein structural dynamics.

PROKR1.functional_summary: PROKR1 functions as a G protein-coupled receptor that binds extracellular signals and transmits these signals across the plasma membrane by activating associated G-proteins, promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP on the alpha subunit. It participates in neuropeptide signaling pathways, where binding of neuropeptides initiates intracellular signaling cascades that regulate downstream cellular processes. PROKR1.gene_summary: PROKR1 encodes prokineticin receptor 1, a G protein-coupled receptor involved in mediating neuropeptide signaling and regulating physiological processes such as circadian rhythm and cellular responses to hormones. SLC17A6.functional_summary: SLC17A6 functions as a neurotransmitter transmembrane transporter that enables the directed movement of L-glutamate across membranes, facilitating glutamatergic synaptic transmission through vesicular release and receptor activation. SNRPN.functional_summary: SNRPN functions in RNA binding and protein binding, specifically interacting with small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles. STS.functional_summary: STS encodes an enzyme with arylsulfatase and steryl-sulfatase activities, catalyzing the hydrolysis of sulfate esters such as phenol sulfates and steroid sulfates. It engages in 122 protein interactions, most notably with HSD3B1, AKR1C3, CYP17A1, HSD3B2, and SULT2B1. Expression of STS is highest in the tibial artery. STS causes X-linked ichthyosis, a condition characterized by skin abnormalities and is also linked to neurological and cardiac phenotypes due to hemizygous deletions encompassing the gene; affected individuals may demonstrate cognitive and mood alterations consistent with neurodevelopmental involvement. The literature on STS spans themes including neurodevelopmental disorders, neuroanatomy and cognition, and genetic and molecular mechanisms, with investigations into neuroimmune interactions and therapeutic interventions.
